SUSPENSION OF QUESTION HOUR 
MR. CHAIRMAN: Question No. 61.  (Interruption). 
 
SHRI PRANAB MUKHERJEE (West Bengal): Mr. Chairman, Sir, I 
have given notice of a motion for the suspension of the Question Hour and I 
would like to draw your attention to a fact which is very serious. It concerns 
not only the individual Members but also the dignity of the House. Sir, 
yesterday, an item was slated in the List of Business that Mr. Ram Jethmalani 
will make a statement explaining the reasons for his resignation from the 
Council of Ministers. That item was ad mitted, it was listed in the List of 
Business. Thereafter, that item did not come, and when the Chair, after 
transacting the business up to the items preceding that item, took up the next 
item, skipping that particular item, I raised a point of order under rule 23 of 
the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of Business in the Council of States and 
wanted to know the reasons why that particular item was skipped. Thereafter, 
we were told that the statement which the Member concerned, here Mr. Ram 
Jethmalani, forwarded to the Rajya Sabha Secretariat at 9.45 A.M., was 
running into hundreds of pages and it contained certain contents, certain 
statements, certains facts, certain observations and certain comments which 
cannot be permitted to be told in the House as per the Rules of Procedure and 
Conduct of Business of this House. Therefore, a peculiar situation was created 
and the Chairman satisfied himself that the statement should not be made 
yesterday and we accepted that position because proviso to rule 23 says that if 
the Chairman is satisfied that there arc reasons for deferring a particular item, 
that can be done and we satisfied ourselves. It was expected that the statement 
would come today because 24 hours have passed. But instead of that, there is 
no mention of that particular statement 
1 

RAJYA SABHA [27 July, 2000] 
in the List of Business for today. We do not know as to what has happened. 
But in between in the morning newspapers, we read: "supposed to be the 
statement, alleged to be the statement," Nobody is there to authenticate and it 
is stated there that he did not resign. He was sacked by the Prime Minister. 
Knowing fully well, Mr. Chairman said that this House has no responsibility 
so far as the Confidence Motion or No Confidence Motion on the Council of 
Ministers is concerned. That is the job of the other House. But surely, this 
House has the right to have information as to what actually happened. We 
thought that we are the privileged one, because the Minister who resigned 
belongs to this House. He will come to this House and explain the reasons 
which compelled him to resign from the Council of Minister, and we were 
quite happy when the statement was recorded that he is going to make a 
statement. Now, not only that, we are told, that too through the newspapers 
again—the Member could have come to the House, could have mentioned it, 
could have tried to take his colleagues into confidence—that if the Rajya 
Sabha does not give him time to make a statement by today, then, he should 
have the option to withdraw his offer. Sir, is Rajya Sabha a bargaining 
Council? Can any Member of this House take this House for granted that he 
would like to make a particular statement and can he fix a deadline that if he is 
not allowed to make his statement by that particular deadline, he withdraws 
his offer? Nobody forced him. As per the practice, the Member concerned 
may opt to make a statement; he may not opt to make a statement. But surely, 
he cannot take the House for granted and make an issue that unless by such 
and such time, he is allowed to make a statement, and if this information 
which you are having is correct, that the contents of the statement which he 
tried to make, cannot be allowed as per the Rules of Procedure and Conduct of 
Business of this House, am I to believe that a senior lawyer, who happened to 
be the Law Minister of the country, did not know the rules of the Rajya Sabha, 
did not know the procedure, did not know what part of the statement can be 
allowed as per rules or what part of the statement cannot be allowed? Is it not 
a case of clear manipulation? If somebody tries to open a bargaining counter    
with     the    Government     or    with     somebody    saying 
2 

[27 July, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
'look, you accommodate me, you try to help me, otherwise, I am going to spill 
the beans', can this forum be used for that purpose? Unless, Mr. Chairman, 
this issue is cleared it will be very difficult for us to transact any business and 
cooperate in the transaction of the business of the House. Now the question is, 
first, the Government comes. Here, the Prime Minister is present; he can 
clarify the position at least on one point, whether Mr. Ram Jethmalani was 
sacked or whether Mr. Ram Jethmala ni resigned from the Council of 
Ministers. At least, somebody should, authoritatively tell us as to what is the 
position. What is the position in regard to the statement? Why has this 
happened? Why these types of statements are coming through newspapers? 
The point is whether there is any remedy so that this House is not 
manipulated and somebody, being a Member of this House, does not use it to 
further his political career or advantage. Till this issue is sorted jut, Mr. 
Chairman, Sir, most respectfully, I would like to submit that let the Question 
Hour be suspended and let the Members give their views. It is a question of 
the prestige and dignity of the House and see how this House is being 
manipulated. It must be resolved; the House should not be allowed to be 
manipulated by any individual, however powerful he or she may be. There 
was no compulsion on Shri Ram Jethmalani to  give a notice to the Rajya 
Sabha Secretariat that 'I would like to make a Statement. He gave a notice. 
Thereafter, he told the Secretariat and many of us are in personal knowledge, 
that he would send the statement sufficiently ahead. At 9.45, this statement 
comes, and this statement contains so many things, which cannot be allowed 
as per the rules. Then what is it but a glaring example of manipulation; 
manipulation to further, the political career and interest of certain individuals. 
Can this august forum be utilised for that? This is matter on which I do hope 
the Members will give their opinion, and this issue should be sorted out. 
Thank you, Mr. Chairman, Sir, for giving me permission and I do hope the 
Question Hour would be suspended and this issue taken up immediately. 
SHRI NILOTPAL BASU (West Benga l): Hon. Chairman, Sir, it is 
indeed very serious to see the turn of events. This is difficulty for us. For 
whatever reasons, this item was listed yesterday. Therefore, 
3 

RAJYA SABHA           [27 July, 2000] 
some authentic version should come, either from the Government or from the 
Chair, as to how the events have happened and how we could allow 
ourselves to be put in this ridiculous position. That Member is claiming 
privately that he has been sacked but the Government is saying that he has 
resigned. Parliament is now in session. Therefore, an authentic version 
should definitely come from the Government, on the floor of the House, 
giving us the details as to how all these things have happened. On the other 
hand, we should clear ourselves about the fact that he cannot be allowed to 
make that personal explanation. It is because of the fact that his statement 
and the procedures he adopted do not comply with the rules of business of 
this House. The position xof the Rajya Sabha, as an institution, gets totally 
undermined. Therefore, Sir, in the interest of this House, to protect the 
traditions of this House and the institution, something has to be done. I think, 
Sir, it will be proper for the Government to explain the position, as well as 
some explanation from the Chair as to how this unfortunate and unseemly 
development has taken place, which is .threatening the very reputation and 
the very prestige of this very great institution.

RESOLUTION 
In order to reduce storage and transit losses of foodgrains at farm and 
commercial level, to modernise the system of handling, storage and 
transportation of the foodgrains procured by the Food Corporation of India 
(FCI) and to bring in additionality of resources through private sector 
involvement, the Government has approved a National Policy on Handling. 
Storage and Transportation of Foodgrains, details of which are given 
below:— 
1. Objective of the Policy 
The main objectives of the policy are: 
i. to reduce storage and transit losses at farm level where about 70% of 
the total foodgrain production is retained and consumed and also to 
encourage the farmers to adopt scientific storage methods. 
ii. to modernise the system of handling, storage and transporatation of 
the foodgrains procured by the Food Corporation of India (FCI). 
iii. to harness efforts and resources of public and private sectors, both 
domestic and foreign, to build and operate infrastructure for introduction of 
bulk handling, storage ant transportation of foodgrains in the country. 
2. Policy for house-hold storage 
2 1 Since the house-hold sector retains about 70% of the total production 
and substantial quantities of foodgrains are wasted due- to 
47 

RAJYA SABHA [27 July, 2000] 
improper storage at farm level, the major focus is on the improvement of 
storage standards at farm level. Presently, the only scheme targeting this need 
is the Save Grain Campaign, which popularises the use of metallic and non-
metallic storage structures and educates the farmers about the adoption of 
scientific storage methods. The scheme also aims at 
development/improvement of non-metallic traditional storage structures. 
2.2 In order to have a greater success in this area, following initiatives 
have been approved:— 
(i) introduction of a scheme to encourage use of metal bins as well as 
non-metallic storage structures at individual farm level and construction of 
RCC bins at community level with appropriate financial incentives. 
(ii) strengthening of the existing research and training components of the 
Save Grain Campaign Scheme for scientific storage and preservation of 
foodgrains and their propagation among 
farmers. 
3.   Modernisation   and   Upgradation   of  Bulk   Grain   Handling 
Infrastructure 
3.1 In order to reduce storage losses, it is necessary to develop and 
modernise the infrastructure for integrated bulk handling storage and 
transportation in India. The thrust of the policy should be:— 
(i) encouragement of mechanical harvesting, cleaning and drying at farm 
and mandi level. 
(ii) transportation of grains from farm to silos by specially designed 
trucks. 
(iii) construction of a chain of silos at procurement as well as 
distribution points. 
(iv) transportation of grain from silos to railhead and thereafter to pre-
determined destinations by specially designed trucks/rail wagons (with top 
filling and bottom discharge mechanism) dedicated trains. 
(v) declaration of foodgrains storage as infrastructure. 
48 

[27 July, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
3.2 For storage of foodgrains procured by the FCI, integrated bulk 
handling facilities with silos of large capacity for wheat along with testing 
facilities for quality control would be created at about 20 identified central 
locations in producing and consuming areas as well as a few port towns. 
These facilities, including the infrastructure for bulk transportation to these 
centres, will be created and maintained in the private sector under the overall 
co-ordination of the FCI. The design of special top filling and bottom 
discharge wagons would be decided in consultation with the Ministry of 
Railways. The Ministry of Railways will also be consulted while deciding the 
locations and the circuits where these wagons would ply. FCI will guarantee 
utilisation of these facilities to the extent of 100% for the first ten years and 
75% for the next ten years. From these points, secondary transportation of 
foodgrains would be made in bag form to about 500 godowns in important 
central locations in different States to be owned and maintained by the FCI. 
Further transportation to the consuming centers for retail distribution under 
the Public Distribution System will be carried out by the State Governments. 
3.3 The private sector will be encouraged to build storage capacities in 
which they will store and maintain foodgrains procured by the Government 
agencies,  for which  they will be entitled to 
storage charges. 
3.4 The private sector participation should be sought and 
encouraged for development of infrastructure for the integrated bulk 
handling, storage and transportation through— 
(i) measures such as Build-Own-Operate-Transfer (BOOT), Build-Own-
Lease-Transfer (BOLT), Build-Own-Operate (BOO), Lease-Develop-Operate 
(LDO), Joint Ventures etc. 
(ii) generation of funds through public issues by private enterprises 
(iii) automatic approval for Foreign Direct Investment (FDI) upto 100%

(a) 100% deduction in profit for the purpose of Income Tax  for the

(b) deduction of 40% of the profit derived by financial institutions 
financing such projects, as provided to financial corporations 
engaged, inter-alia, in providing long term finance for agricultural 
development. 
(c) customs duty exemption for items not manufactured in India, on a 
case-to-case basis, subject to a list of such equipment being 
submitted in advance. 
4. Development of Infrastructure Facilities at Ports 
India has been traditionally the importer of foodgrains and, therefore, the 
infrastructure facilities available at the ports are basically meant for unloading 
operations and not for exports. For unloading operations, ship gears are 
normally used. Even the latest machanised facilities at Jawaharlal Nehru Port, 
Navi Mumbai have been designed for import purposes only. There is also lack 
of general cargo berths at the major ports and very limited warehousing 
facilities are available for the storage of foodgrains at ports. For creating the 
proper port facilities for foodgrains meant for export in due course, the 
infrastructure facilities would have to be developed for which following 
actions are required: 
(i) identification of ports to be developed for purposes of export of 
foodgrains. The distribution of foodgrains traffic may spread over to the 
non-traditional ports which have spare capacity like New Mangalore and 
Cochin ports; (ii) development of more general cargo berths at the ports 
through ports' own investment/private participation; (iii) water 
front/berths can be leased to the users who may be encouraged to put up 
their own facilities; and 
50 

[27 July, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
(iv) development of dedicated modern foodgrains handling facilities at 
selected ports. 
5. Role of the Central Government 
The Central Government would: 
(a) facilitate speedy clearance of projects concerning development 
of infrastructure for bulk handling, transportation and storage of 
foodgrains by setting up an Approval Board competent to take final 
decision; 
(b) enter   into    bilateral    agreements   with    other   countries/ 
international agencies for providing technical/financial assistance; 
(c) take necessary legislative / administrative measures for 
removing   impediments   with   regard   to   stock   control   orders/ 
movement control orders framed by various State Governments; 
(d) utilize the services of an existing independent regulatory mechanism 
for fixing/regulating tariff for various operations, such as cleaning, drying, 
storage; transportation, etc.; 
(e) make     available     facilities    of    the    Railways    for    bulk 
transportation; 
(f) promote negotiable Warehouse Receipt System by which 
farmers could hold their grains back from market and meet their 
working capital/short term requirement by borrowing from Banks 
against these receipts; and 
(g) promote research for development of alternate storage 
technologies like Vacuum Process Storage (VPS) technology which 
would ensure longer shelf life of foodgrains and help export of 
foodgrains in vacuum packs. 
6. Role of State Government 
The State Government would help in: 
(a) acquisition of land required for various projects as for public 
purpose; and

[27 July, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
THE MINISTER OF EXTERNAL AFFAIRS (SHRI JASWANT 
SINGH): (a) to (c) The "SAARC Vision Beyond the Year 2000" is the title of 
the Report of the SAARC Group of Eminent. Persons-(GEP) established by 
the Ninth SAARC Summit to undertake a comprehensive appraisal of 
SAARC and identify measures to further enhance the effectiveness of the 
Association. The leaders also decided that the Group should develop a long-
range vision and formulate a perspective plan of action including a SAARC 
Agenda for 2000 and Beyond. 
The GEP's recommendations focused on 3 areas: 
I. A time bound plan for regional economic integration, including 
negotiation of a Treaty for a South Asian Free Trade Area (SAFTA) by 
1999, with implementation commencing in 2000 and achievement of a full 
SAFTA in 2008 for SAARC members and 2010 for SAARC LDCs; 
II. Adoption of a Social Charter for SAARC incorporating social welfare 
targets in the areas of population stabilisation, universal primary    
education,    empowerment    of    women,  poverty 
eradication,    human    resource    development,    and    health 
promotion, nutrition and protection of children; 
III. Reform of SAARC institutions. 
In the Economic field, it also envisaged a SAARC Customs Union, with 
harmonisation of external tariffs by 2015, and a SAARC Economic Union, 
with harmonisation of monetary and fiscal policies by 2020. The GEP 
recommended special measures for the Least Developed Countries to enable 
them to adjust to a Free Trade Area. 
Action taken on the GEP Report was as follows: 
SSARC leaders at the 10th SAARC Submit at Colombo held in July 
1998 accepted two of the GEP's main recommendations—(i) achieving 
SAFTA and (ii) the adoption of a SAARC Social Charter. The leaders agreed 
to set up a Committee of Experts with specific terms of reference for drafting 
a comprehensive, treaty regime for 
53 

RAJYA SABHA [27 July, 2000] 
creating a free trade area by 2001. 
The other recommendations in the GEP Report were considered by the 
SAARC Standing Committee of Foreign Secretaries and Council of Ministers 
in Nuwara Eliya in March 1999. There was however no consensus on the long 
term goals of a SAARC Customs Union by 2015 and SAARC Economic 
Union by 2020. It was agreed that these issues would be further discussed. 
The First Meeting of the Committee of Experts on SAFTA was held on 
July 15—17, 1999, in Kathmandu at which its Terms of Reference were 
agreed upon. The second meeting is scheduled to be helf in Kathmandu on 
mutually agreed dated. India has conveyed its agreement to participation in 
the meeting. An Intergovernmental Expert Group is also proposed to be set up 
to commence work on the Social Charter. 
Following the military coup in Pakistan a decision was taken after 
mutual consultations among SAARC member States to postpone the 11th 
SAARC Summit scheduled to be held on November, 26—28, 1999 in 
Kathmandu, Nepal. It may be recalled that Pakistan was also suspended from 
the Commonwealth's decisionmaking Councils and this suspension continues. 
However, postponement of the Summit does to impinge on technical and 
functional cooperation, and SAARC meetings continue to be held at the 
technical and official levels. Thus the following meetings, which India has 
participated in, have taken place: 
1. "Financing Renewable Energy for Sustainable Development and 
Alleviation of Rural Energy Poverty in South Asia", June 12—14, 2000 
Colombo. This meeting was organised under the joint aegis of the World 
Energy Council and SAARC. 
2. 6th Meeting of the Governing Board of the South Asian 
Development Fund (SADF), May 22-23, 2000 Maldives. 
3. First meeting of the Technical Committee on Agriculture and rural 
Development under the restructured Integrated Programme of Action. July 4-
5, 2000, Kathmandu.

508. SHRI NAGENDRA NATH OJHA  
 SHRI R.S.  GAVAI: 
Will the Minister of CONSUMER AFFAIRS AND PUBLIC 
DISTRIBUTION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether any proposal to drastically lower the retirement age for 
workers in the Food Corporation of India to 45 years from 60 years is under 
consideration of Government; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) the reasons for lowering the retirement age; 
 
(d) whether FCI workers union has been consulted in this regard; and 
(e) if so, the views expressed by them? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF CONSUMER 
AFFAIRS AND PUBLIC DISTRIBUTION (SHRI SHRIRAM CHAUHAN): 
(a) to (c) While considering the issue of organisational restructuring of the 
Food Corporation of India with specific reference to manpower management, 
Government has directed the Corporation to examine the matter regarding the 
age of retirement for its workers as per the Standing Orders, issued by the 
Ministry of Labour in this regard and discuss it with the workers Unions 
thereafter. Government is of the view that it would be in the overall interest 
of the workers as well as the Corporation if the retirement age of the workers 
could be brought down to around 45 years keeping in view the hazardous 
nature of work the workers are to perform. 
(d) and (e) The FCI is yet to examine the matter. It has been instructed 
to examine the issue of reduction in age of labour separately and, thereafter, 
to discuss with the Unions. The FCI Workers Union in its representation of 
27.6.2000 has, inter-alia, suggested that the FCI management, instead of 
adopting the measure of reducing the age of retirement to 45 years from 60 
years, should concentrate in taking corrective steps like semi mechanisation 
of the work by installing fork, lift etc. and by reducing the work load norms

Programme 
535. SHRI PREM CHAND GUPTA:

what action Government are taking to solicit for more meaningful 
response from the US? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF EXTERNAL 
AFFAIRS (SHRI AJIT KUMAR PANJA): (a) After the end of the Cold War,

AFFAIRS (SHRI AJIT KUMAR PANJA): (a) Pakistan has received nuclear

Sri Lanka-India Joint Statement 
(June 12, 2000) 
The Minister of External Affairs of India, Shri Jaswant Singh made an 
official visit to Sri Lanka, at the invitation of the Government of Sri Lanka, 
from 11th to 12th Jane. During his visit the Minister had discussions with 
President Kumaratunga and Foreign Minister, Lakshman Kadirgamar. He also 
met Mr. Ranil Wickremesinghe, the Leader of the Opposition and 
representatives from other political parties. 
At the commencement of discussions, the visiting Minister reiterated the 
continued commitment of the Government of India to the unity, sovereignty 
and territorial integrity of Sri Lanka. He also expressed the good wishes and 
support of the Government of India to the restoration of a lasting peace, which 
would be possible through a political process that produces a settlement, 
which meets the aspirations of all communities. 
The discussions touched upon the present situation and also the broader 
issues related to the further strengthening of the existing close and friendly 
relations that India and Sri Lanka have traditionally enjoyed. 
President Kumaratunga apprised the visiting Minister of current political   
developments   including   the   consultations   between   the 
164 

[27 July 2000] RAJYA   SABHA 
Government and other political parties and the facilitation efforts of Norway. 
President Kumaratunga welcomed India's offer to be of assistance in the 
humanitarian as well as economic sphere to ease any constraints that may be 
currently faced by Sri Lanka. Shri Jaswant Singh added in this regard that 
India would be prepared to extend to. Sri Lanka a credit facility, on terms to 
be mutually worked out between the two Finance Ministers, amounting to 
USS 100 million. The possibilities of Sri Lanka's purchasing wheat, rice and 
sugar on a counter trade basis from India, were also discussed. 
In conclusion both sides noted that the discussions had been productive 
and that they had enabled the reaching of understandings on the measures 
that India and Sri Lanka can take both collectively as well as individually, to 
bring about lasting peace in Sri Lanka. Shri Jaswant Singh emphasised that he 
was leaving Sri Lanka at the end of his visit confident of the depth, strength 
and direction of India-Sri Lanka relations and their ability to meet the 
common challenges both countries face.

Core level standard fixed by ILO 
576. SHRI RAMACHANDRA KHUNTIA:  Will the Minister of 
LABOUR be pleased to state; 
(a) whether Government are rectifying all seven core level standard 
fixed by ILO; and 
(b) by when Government propose to bring these legislations in 
Parliament? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF LABOUR AND 
EMPLOYMENT (SHRI MUNI LALL): (a) and (b) Among the 8 ILO core 
Conventions, India has ratified 4, namely, Convention No. 29 concerning 
Equal Remuneration, Convention No. 105 concerning Abolition of Forced 
Labour and Convention No. 111 concerning Discrimination (Employment and 
Occupation). A Central Legislation is proposed to be enacted fixing a 
minimum age for admission to employment which should facilitate ratification 
of Convention No. 138 concerning Minimum Age for Admission to 
Employment at a later stage on achieving satisfactory compliance to the 
proposed legislation. Tripartite and inter-ministerial consultation are in

concerning the Worst Forms of Child Labour. The rights guaranteed under 
Convention No. 87 concerning Freedom of Association and Right to Organise 
and No. 98 concerning Right to Organise and Collective Bargaining are, by 
and large, available to all workers in the country. India has not been able to 
ratify these two conventions because of the reasonable restrictions imposed 
on Government servants. The constitutionality and the reasonableness of 
these restrictions have been upheld by the highest courts in India. Therefore, 
at this stage, there is no proposal to ratify these two Conventions. The 
Parliament will be informed as and when the Government propose to ratify an 
ILO Convention.

Employment and Social Security Measures 
579. SHRI KARNENDU BHATTACHARJEE: Will the Minister of 
LABOUR be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that in its World Labour Report, 2000 the 
International Labour Organisation (ILO) has expressed serious concern about 
absence of unemployment protection and social security measures in the 
developing countries including India; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; and 
(c) the steps proposed to be taken to improve the existing level of 
social security measures including special old age provisions and health care 
schemes? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN TH E MINISTRY OF LABOUR AND 
EMPLOYMENT (SHRI MUNI LALL): (a ) to (c) ILO's World Labour 
Report, 2000 examined the vital role played by social protection in supporting, 
supplementing and replacing market incomes in the event of old age, 
incapacity for work and unemployment. The Report says that but for those 
who work in the rural or urban sectors in developing countries, there is hardly 
any unemployment protection at all. The Report notes that major Asian 
countries like India have social and health insurance schemes covering 
millions of workers and their families, but the vast majority of the population 
in developing countries, including informal sector wage earners and self-
employed persons have no social protection whatsoever and suggests that the 
major focus must be on the extension of the coverage of these workers. 
At present, there are two major social security schemes in India, namely, 
the Employees Provident Fund Scheme and the Employees State Insurance 
Scheme. However, the benefits of these two schemes arc by and large 
confined to the workers of the organised sector. The 
183 

RAJYA SABHA [27 July, 2000] 
recently introduced pension scheme under the Employees Provident Fund 
Scheme is also meant-to take care of the retired workers in their old age. 
Besides, many State Governments have introduced old age and destitute 
pension schemes. Social security for the workers in the informal sector is by 
and large confined to some welfare measures. The scope and coverage of 
these welfare schemes will expanded from time to time. However, it is not 
possible, at this stage, with the present stage of economic development to 
provide comprehensive unemployment insurance and benefits to all sections 
of the work force.

The Rules for the Allocation of Business of the Government are made by 
the President under Clause (3) of Article 77 of the Constitution for 
convenient transaction of business of the Government. The business to be 
transacted in various Ministries and Departments is specified in the 
Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961. Each Department

under the Allocation of Business Rules, is disposed of under the general or 
special directions of, the Minister-in-charge of the Department. The number 
of Ministries/Departments at a given point of time is thus based on the 
administrative convenience of the Government.

(SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) to (e) The Rules for the Allocation of 
Business of the Government are made by the President under Clause (3) of 
Article 77 of the Constitution for convenient transaction of business of the 
Government. The business to be transacted in various Ministries and 
Departments is specified in 
195 

RAJYA SABHA [27 July, 2000] 
the Government of India (Allocation of Business) Rules, 1961. Each 
Department is under the charge of a Minister and the business allocated to the 
Department under the Allocation of Business Rules, is disposed of under the 
general or special directions of the Minister-in-charge of the Department. The 
number of Ministries-Departments at a given point of time is thus based on

and Subordinate Offices, etc. in consultation with the Ministry of Finance

is completed, no vacant posts will be filled up except with the approval of the 
Ministry of Finance (Department of Expenditure). Further, such 
Ministries/Departments as had not fully implemented the Government's earlier 
decision to achieve 10% reduction in the number of posts (as on 1.1.1992)

information available with the Ministry of Finance, approximately 1.83 lakh

Growing Imbalance in the Economic Progress of the States 
606. SHRI B J. PANDA: Will the PRIME MINISTER be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether the pace of progress of each State differs from other and 
some States arc remaining backward;" 
(b) if so, the reasons for the growing imbalance in the economic 
progress of the States; 
(c) the steps taken to identify the bottleneck and remove the regional 
imbalance so that the backward States develop at par with the advanced 
States; and 
(d) the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING, 
MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF STATISTICS AND 
PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION, MINISTER OF STATE OF THE 
DEPARTMENT OF ADMINISTRATIVE   REFORMS   AND   PUBLIC   
GRIEVANCES 
212 

[27 July, 2000] RAJYA SABHA 
OF THE MINISTRY OF PERSONNEL, PUBLIC GRIEVANCES AND 
PENSIONS AND MINISTER OF STATE OF THE DEPARTMENT OF 
DISINVESTMENT (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. There are 
certain regions in the country which have not been able to benefit adequately 
from the overall growth process. Growth and development are intimately 
related to the level of economic integration of the various parts of the country and 
the linkages that are formed between the backward and the more developed 
regions. For the most part such regions reflect the inadequate integration of the 
local economics in the wider growth process due to resource constraints, fiscal 
barriers, barriers in inter-State commerce, poor provision of social 
infrastructure, in some instances poor governance etc. 
(c) and (d) Balanced regional development has always been an essential 
component of the Indian Development Strategy. Since not all parts of the 
country are equally well endowed to take advantage of growth opportunities 
and since historical inequalities have not been eliminated, planned 
intervention is required. Planning and Development of an area and allocation 
of funds are primarily th e responsibility of concerned State Governments. 
However, Central Government supplements the efforts of the State 
Governments in dealing with the special problems of designated areas 
through the allocation of Central assi stance and special Central assistance. 
Normal Central assistance for the Annual Plans of States is allocated based on 
the Gadgil formula approved by NDC in December, 1991. The formula inter-
alia gives weightage to population and per capita income so as to ensure 
adequate allocation of Central assistance to backward States and overall 
regional balance. Special Central assistance is given for addressing specific 
problems of certain regions e.g. Hill Area Development Programme 
(HADP)/Western Ghats Development Programme (WGDP) and the Border 
Area Development Programme (BADP).

SCALE INDUSTRIES AND AGRO AND RURAL INDUSTRIES 
(SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE): (a) and (b) Government has approved 
a Credit Guarantee Fund Scheme for Small Scale Industries (CGFSI). To 
begin with a corpus of Rs. 125 Crores  is being created of which Rs. 100 
Crores would be contributed by the Government of India and Rs. 25 Crores

banks to Small Scale Industrial units, without collaterals including third party 
guarantees.

Danger to the Country's Security 
† 617. SHRI VIJAY SINGH YADAV: Will the PRIME MINISTER be 
pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that American companies have free access 
to vital organisation like atomic and defence organisations in the 
name of satellite imaging; 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(c) whether it has endangered the security of the country; and 
(d) if so, what action is being taken by Government? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE DEPARTMENT OF SPACE 
(SHRIMATI VASUNDHARA RAJE)i (a) and (b) No, Sir. American 
Companies have only access to take imagery from Outer Space, which is 
beyond our sovereign air space. 
(c) and (d) No, Sir. Imaging capabili ties from space and the consequent 
availability' of such information by other countries has already been a factor, 
which was reckoned in our security planning. Government has also been aware 
of the worldwide commercial remote sensing developments and has taken 
measures to regulate the acquisition and distribution of data within the 
country. In addition, Government has also taken steps to further enhance our 
own space remote sensing capabilities.

(d) whether persons responsible for the cost/time overrun have been

THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF PLANNING, 
MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF STATISTICS AND 
PROGRAMME IMPLEMENTATION, MINISTER OF STATE IN THE 
DEPARTMENT OF' ADMINISTRATIVE REFORMS AND PUBLIC 
GRIEVANCES OF THE MINISTRY OF PERSONNEL, PUBLIC 
GRIEVANCES AND PENSIONS, AND MINISTER OF STATE OF THE 
DEPARTMENT OF DISINVESTMENT (SHRI ARUN SHOURIE): (a) and 
(b) Yes, Sir, As on 31.3.2000, out of 473 projects, 216 have shown cost 
overruns and also time overrun. As against the original cost of Rs. 1,25,459.3 
crores for 473 projects, anticipated cost is Rs. 1,70,063.8 crores, showing a cost 
overrun of 35.6%. The costs of projects are approved at the prices prevailing 
in particular months and years. The cost overruns take place with reference to 
current prices due to general escalation; The cost overruns also take place due 
to delays, increase in scope and variations in duties, wages etc. The sector-
wise details are given in the annexed Statement (See below). 
(c) The steps taken to remove the bottlenecks responsible for delay in 
the completion of the projects are as follows: 
(i) Monthly as well as quarterly monitoring by the Government. This 
enables the monitoring agencies to identify constrains and help the   
management/administrative   Ministries   in   taking   remedial 
measures; 
240

(ii) In-depth review of progress by the Project Authorities and Administrative 
Ministries, coordination with the respective State Governments, equipment 
suppliers, engineering a nd procurement contractors, project management 
consultants and other concerned agencies; 
(iii) Inter-ministerial coordination and holding facilitation meetings 
among concerned agencies; 
(iv) Setting up of Empowered Committees for speedy finalisation of 
contract packages, solving of land acquisition and other problems; and 
(v) Making funds available to complete the projects on schedule. 
(d) In order to bring accountability in the execution of projects, Standing 
Committees have been set up in 22 Ministries for projects costing Rs.50 
crores and above, which have reported time and cost overruns, headed by 
Additional Secretary or Joint Secretary of the concerned Ministry with 
representatives from Planning Commission, Department of Expenditure and 
Ministry of Statistics & Programme Implementation. The Standing 
Committees, set up as per the guidelines of the Planning Commission issued 
in August, 1998, have the mandate, to go into the details of time and cost 
overrun and to identify the respective responsibility areas and to suggest 
remedial action. The repo rts of the Standing Comm ittees form part of the 
revised cost estimates of projects which have time and cost overruns and the 
same are submitted, along with the CCEA note, for consideration of the 
CCEA. So far 40 cases have been referred to these Committees. Out of 10 
cases examined by the Committees, only in one case responsibility has been 
fixed, while in others, the Committees have identified the agencies and 
system weaknesses responsible for delays and cost overruns.

SHORT DURATION DISCUSSION 
Disinvestment Policy of The Government 
SHRI J. CHITHARANJAN (Kerala): Mr. Chairman, Sir, I am 
going to raise a discussion on the disinvestment policy of the 
Government, which is an issue of great national importance. Now, the 
Vajpayee Government has changed the policy with regard to 
disinvestment, of course, the disinvestment policy was announced and 
started in 1991. But as Mr. Arun Jaitley himself has said now a 
qualitative and quantitative change has taken place with regard to that 
policy. Now, what they are saying is that instead of piecemeal 
disinvestment, unit-wise and sectoral-wise disinvestment is being 
carried on, and to say the truth, in fact, an aggressive disinvestment is 
being carried on. 
In fact, it seems that the real aim is to demolish and dismantle 
the huge edifice of public sector industries and to privatise them. Such 
a step will be against the national interest of our country. The public 
sector was started on the basis of the Industrial Policy Resolution 
adopted in 1966. Immediately after attaining freedom, the question of 
industrialisation, the question of economic development and such other 
issues had to be tackled. Therefore, in a condition when the 
industrialists of our country were not able to invest enough money for 
industrialisation or budding up the infrastructure, it was felt that the 
Government would have to enter the field in a big way. Thus, these 
public institutions were started, in the past several decades a massive 
investment, nearly Rs. 2.00,000 crores, has been made in the public 
sector. It is a very huge amount. A very big public sector edifice has 
been built up.  Those industries are engaged in producing 
248 

[27 JULY. 2000] RAJYA SABHA  
a variety qf products. I don't want to go into the details. This pubic sector 
has made an immense contribution to the development of our nation and 
the development of our economy. Nowadays,  moat of our Ministers, 
especially the Finance Minister are claiming again and again that India is 
now one among the first dozen industrialised countries in the whole 
world If he is able to claim that, it is because of the development of pubic 
sector industries In the whole country. Now. It Is being scandelled.It is 
being mallgned. to a great extent. One argument  that is put forward Is 
that the objectives, whatever be the objectives, of pubic sector industries 
have not bean achieved during the test several decades. That is one of 
the arguments that has been raised. Another argument Is that the profit 
ratio is very less. Regarding that, firstly. I would like to point out that 
though an amount of Rs.2.00.000 crores has bean invested, the actual 
equity put in the 1996-97 was only Rs55.000 crores. The rest has bean 
taken as loans and these loans have already been paid back. If you look 
at the other results of the pubic sector, you will find that the number of 
enterprises have gone up from 5 in 1961 with an investment of Rs.29 
crores to 246 In. 1995-96. There was a substantial increase in the gross 
sales of these enterprises The net profit of these units have also 
increased. For example, in 1994-96 the net profit was Rs.7,187 crores. 
In the next year, it has gone up to Rs.9.878 crores. There was en 
increase of 37.44 par cent. The value added in production was 25.4%. 
The gross internal resources had also increased by 21.9 per cent, in the 
case of export earning, it has increase ' by 15.1 percent. The value of 
inventories has also been brought down from 77 days of cost of 
production to 70 days. Trie contribution to the exchequer by way of 
corporate tax, excise duty, customs duty, other duties and dividend. all 
together, has gone up to Rs.32.096 crores in 1996-97 and it has further 
increased in the following years. 
Then the expenditure on social overheads has also increased. 
The 
number of houses for the employees has increased. The average annua 
emoluments of the workers and employees has Increased. The number 
of regular employees is 20 lakhs. Two million workers are employed in 
the pubic sector. In fact, the public sector has made tremendous 
contributor towar ds building up the economy and In the field of 
Industrialisation. At the same time, the gross value of the assets has 
increased very much. Though we have Invested only Rs. 65,000 crores, 
the assets of ten major public sector undertakings atone would come to 
Rs. 5 lakhs crore. Therefore, the has also increased. Then we also have 
to take into consideration various other contributions which the pubic 
sector has made by way of substituting imports and also by producing 
various items, especialy important machinery which we had to import 
eerier. These are some of the contibution which the pubic sector has 
made.   What are the circumstances 
249 

RAJYA SABHA [27JULY. 2000]  
compelled or persuaded the Government to disinvest  institutions and 
privatise .them as early as possible? I cannot' understand it, in fact, the 
argument that is being given is this. The argument is that the budgetary 
support which the Government has been giving involves a very huge amount 
which cannot be continued; If we go into the facts, the facts show that 
the budgetary allocation that has 'been made in the past is only a 
percentage of the contribution Which the public sector is making. 
Therefore, they cannot give this argument. The second argument 
which they have given, is that these institutions will have to be 
modernised further which requires more money. IT you see the figures, 
Rs. 18000 to 19,000 crores have already been realised thr ough 
disinvestment, where has this amount been spent? This amount has not 
been spent on modernising any of the public sector undertakings. This 
amount has not-been utilised for further expanding any of the public 
sector undertakings. This amount has been mainly utilised for meeting 
the budgetary deficit.' That is what is taking place. The Finance Minister 
has already made it clear in his Budget speech that Rs. 10,000 crores 
would be realised through disinvestment. Later on, he said that he 
would like to increase this amount further. He said that Rs. 17,000 crores 
would be realised. Anyhow, a huge amount Is intended to be realised 
through disinvestment this year.. For what? Is it for modernisation of any 
of the public sector' undertakings? Is it for starting any new industry?. 
Or is it for expanding any of the public sector undertakings? No, Sir It is 
only meant for meeting the budgetary deficint. At the same time, when 
you do that, certain institutions which are already making' some 
contribution to the exchequer, a substantial contribution to the exchequer, 
that source is also lost. In the- coming years from where will you .get this 
amount? They do not think about It. Therefore, the policy, that is being 
adopted regarding disinvestment and selling of public sector undertakings 
to private parties, whether it be called a strategic sale or whatever it 
may be. is not- in the interest of the country. It is not in the interest of 
the workers. It is not in the interest of the people as a whole. 
Sir, recently, the Minister of Disinvestment -- until a few days back, 
Shri Jaitley was the Minister— was speaking in an Indo-U.S. business 
meeting where he declared that he would ensure flat "in worker lost his job 
even after disinvestment. Sir, is it true? During the last two wars atone, 
around two lakh workers have been sent  under VBS: this year. The 
number has further increased, and in the coming years it will increase 
manifold. Now the Government has declared that even in the nationalised 
banks,the VRS could be given to the employees; also in  the telecom 
sector, in the Railways, and everywhere," they are declaring VRS. 
Therefore, more and more people are being thrown out of employment. 
Then, how can you say that no worker will lose his job?   And they are 
not being provided with 
250 

[27 JULY, 2000] RAJYA SABHA  
employment elsewhere. It was also said by the Minister in that meeting 
that apart from the VRS benefit, the Government would also come 
forward with a social welfare net scheme. But no such scheme has 
been brought forth so far. And he has said that the scheme would be 
very attractive. But where is the scheme? What are the details of it? 
None of us knows it. Then, regarding the workers working in the public 
sector units, they are not being consulted at all. Their organisations are 
not being consulted. In fact, the Standing Committee on Labour, in its 
36th meeting held on 9 th February, 2000, adopted a resolution noting 
the growing trend towards disinvestment and privatisation. The 
Committee recommended that the concerned Ministries as well as the 
Minister of Disinvestment should consult the tripartite bodies before 
taking decisions with regard to disinvestment in Central public sector 
undertakings as the decision of the Government has implications on 
employment and social security of the workers. This Resolution was 
passed in February, but up till now neither the Minister holding the 
Disinvestment portfolio nor the Finance Minister nor the Prime Minister 
had convened any meeting with the representatives of the trade unions 
for having consultations with them. Nothing has been done. But, of 
course, the Ministers are giving special considerations to the 
employers, and they are always attending some seminar or meeting 
convened by the associations like the Cll, FICCI, ASSOCHAM and so 
on, and they make their policy declarations there. But the trade unions 
are not consulted at all. This is the position. Even the recently-elected 
Chairman of the ASSOCHAM has said to the Press, "Till some time 
back we had to knock at the doors of the Ministers so that we might get 
an opportunity to meet them and make our representations. But there 
is a drastic change now; our position has Changed. Now we are being 
called and consulted; our views are being recognised 'and our 
suggestions are being implemented to the extent possible." This is 
what he said. The status of the employers in this country since 
liberalisation, has been strengthened. At the same time workers are 
not being given proper consideration. They are not being consulted in 
vital matters like this. Even otherwise, take into account the people as 
a whole. This money had been invested by the State. It is the public 
money. It belongs to the people of the whole country. When this is so, 
decisions cannot be taken by one or two people in the Cabinet or by 
the Cabinet in a light way. This is a matter about which a public 
discussion will have to take place. But no such serious discussion has 
ever taken place so far. And I request that, before proceeding with 
disinvestment, the Government shou ld take effective measures for 
having a serious discussion on the whole gamut of issues in the Rajya 
Sabha, the Lok Sabha and in the public as a whole. A national debate 
should take place. That is the first thing.   In the same way, the workers 
should also be consulted.

Regarding disinvestment, it .seems that the Government has not 
declared any policy as such. An experiment is being done, with 
changes being made ovary now and then. . in the beginning, a 
Disinvestment Commission, was constituted. By 1999, its term lapsed 
and   that 
Commission was also dissolved.. Thereafter, no such commission has 
come 
into existence. At the same time, for some time, the Prime Minister's 
Office 
had taken upon itself the whole responsibility. Later, the Disinvestment 
Ministry is formed and somebody is put in its charge, and,every now 
and 
then Ministry is being changed. The way in which the whole thing is 
bein.3 
done is very inept and without any seriously considered and chalked 
out 
programme. It is on that basis that it is being done. If this is continued, 
what will happen is that the. public sector, which has been built up with 
public money, will be demolished. It is a huge edifice. Not only that; 
what 
has- really happened is that, during the last two or three decades, the 
situation in India was that it was the public sector which was giving 
more 
employment opportunities. The private sector was giving very jess 
employment. Today, because the public sector is being dismantled, the 
employment opportunities will not only become less, but lakhs and 
lakhs of 
workers, who are already employed, will lose their jobs and, at the 
seme 
time, in the private sector, more employment opportunities will not be 
generated. That is what is happening. Some of the private sector 
industries and the small-scale sector are lacing a crisis. Tens of 
thousands 
of small-scale industries are being closed. Now, with the lifting of the 
ban 
on imports and also the quantitative re strictions that were imposed, a 
very 
serious situation had arisen. It had affected several industries in our 
country, especially, the small scale industries and it had affected the 
agricultural sector also. We all know that the tobacco cultivators had 
represented to the Prime Minister that they should be allowed not to 
cultivate tobacco during this year, and they were allowed. Therefore, 
what 
will happen in those areas is that there wilt be terrific unemployment. 
The 
unemployment wilt increase. The same thing is happening in other 
cases 
where prices of other commodities are also going down. Therefore, all 
these things will lead to further increase in unemployment. So, 
immediate 
measures will nave to be taken to  find a solution to this problem. 
Therefore, my suggestion is that, not only the question of 
disinvestment, but 
the question of new economic reforms — whether we calf it the second 
stage of reforms or whatever — will have to be reviewed, taking into 
consideration the real situation that is obtaining in the 
country and a solution found. That is what I have to say. Regarding the 
public sector, I would appeal to the Government, through the hon. 
Chairman 
that this attempt at disinvestment should be stopped for the time being, 
the 
matter should be seriously considered and a public debate should take 
place. 252
